Its rules were published in Sid Sackson's A Gamut of Games. There are some commercial versions available though. The object of LoA is to get all your pieces into a single connected group. A group of pieces is connected if they occupy an unbroken chain of adjacent spaces, horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. [Rating: 2/10] I can't imagine trying to play this without a computer telling me where each piece can move, as it's annoyingly difficult just to visualize the available moves; try to think several moves ahead for each of them and you will die.

[Rating: 4/10] This one is a bit too fluid for me to get a handle on.  Basically any piece can move at any time and the goal is not easily seen by me.  This makes it hard to move to stop another person, but perhaps I'd need more plays to figure it out.

[Rating: 4/10] I quite like the line movement dynamics; they make pieces that are potentially across the board meaningful in a local sense, and they make things like connection order useful. And after playing it, I thought the rules did work with a reasonable degree of elegance. (Before playing, I thought the "can jump over your own pieces, but can only land on opponents" rule needlessly complex. But I see how it enables blocking and connection in a way that "you can always jump" or "you can never jump" doesn't.)  My problem was the way movement was used. [Rating: 4/10] Really wasn’t a fan of this one and found it very boring. Ayu does unification better and Hex and Tak do connection better.

[Rating: 4.5/10] Play this over any game of checkers.  Its puzzley, but there is depth to the game.

[Rating: 5/10] If you are into abstract games this would be considered a modern classic.  If you aren't it will be a bit boring.  There are many factors to take into account.  It seems like you really could take 10 minutes figuring out what the best move is, but it would only give you a little bit of an edge over a 30 second move.  Still it may be the winning edge.  Not a bad game at all, but certainly not for me.

[Rating: 5/10] I think for this game (and for abstracts in general) I need to find the right opponent who won't just crush me in a handful of moves.  I like the ideas here that restrict your movement, but I have a difficult time planning ahead, which seems to pretty much spell out doom.

[Rating: 5/10] I've developed somewhat of an interest in this game, however there appears to be a somewhat significant first player advantage, which hampers my willingness to pursue it further. Perhaps variants using larger boards would help to mitigate this.

[Rating: 5/10] Neat that this can be played with any old draughts board, and it's a good game, but it never really got me excited. I discovered [thing=2125][/thing] at the same time and that captured my imagination to a much greater degree.

[Rating: 5/10] something in the simple design doesnt grab me, still if you like abstracts give it a try, it definitely has lots if tactics

[Rating: 5/10] Next time the only thing you have is a set of checkers....don't despair.  Learn and play the game Lines of Action.  It's not a bad abstract game using only the components of a checker set.
